text: California State University, East Bay (Cal State East Bay, CSU East Bay, or CSUEB) is a public university located in Hayward, California, and is part of the California State University system. It offers 136 undergraduate and 60 post-baccalaureate areas of study, with a student body of approximately 11,544 as of Spring 2025 and 760 faculty as of Fall 2024. The university's main campus is in Hayward, on a plateau east of the Hayward fault, with additional centers in Oakland and Concord. Originally established in 1957 as State College for Alameda County (Alameda State College) to serve Alameda and Contra Costa Counties, its initial site was planned in Pleasanton before being moved to Hayward due to advocacy by State Assembly member Carlos Bee and community leaders including S.E. Bond Jr. and E. Guy Warren, whose name is associated with Warren Hall. Classes began at Sunset High School and later Hayward High School in 1959. The university changed its name to Alameda County State College in 1961, then to California State College at Hayward in 1963, received university status in 1972 becoming California State University, Hayward, and adopted its current name, California State University, East Bay, in 2005 after approval by the CSU Board of Trustees on January 26, 2005. Cathy Sandeen, an Oakland native and alumna of Humboldt State University and San Francisco State University, became the sixth president on January 4, 2021, following her appointment announced on October 29, 2020; she previously served as chancellor of the University of Alaska Anchorage and the University of Wisconsin Colleges and University of Wisconsin-Extension from 2014 to 2018. Warren Hall, the university's signature building and a prominent landmark, was rated the least earthquake-safe structure in the CSU system and was demolished by implosion on August 17, 2013, after the CSU Board of Trustees authorized $50 million for its replacement. Construction of the new 67,000-square-foot building began in November 2013 and opened in December 2015. The university is known for its Solar Energy Project, featuring solar panels on four rooftops to generate supplemental power during peak times, making it one of the largest photovoltaic systems in Northern California. On April 8, 2010, the California Public Utilities Commission approved a fuel cell project by Pacific Gas and Electric Company (PG&E) enabling the Hayward campus to become one of the first in Northern California to have a fuel cell, with waste heat converted into hot water for campus use. Since 2004, the Pioneer Amphitheatre has hosted the KBLX Stone Soul Picnic, a festival of R&B, soul, and Urban Adult Contemporary music featuring artists such as Ronald Isley, The Whispers, Teena Marie, Rick James, and The O'Jays, and the Associated Students Incorporated (ASI) hosts concerts with performers like Lupe Fiasco and Goapele. In 2005, the university began construction of three facilities: the Wayne and Gladys Valley Business and Technology Center (VBT), a Pioneer Heights student housing expansion, and a University Union annex. The 67,000-square-foot VBT center was dedicated in February 2007, marking the first new academic building on the Hayward campus in over 30 years and housing programs in business, technology management, engineering, multimedia, science, and online degrees. The Pioneer Heights expansion was dedicated in fall 2008, adding over 450 new student residences and a 16,000-square-foot dining commons, while the University Union annex opened in January 2007. The campus hosts the C. E. Smith Museum of Anthropology, established in 1975, which features rotating exhibits and archives of 18 Bay Area archaeological sites. The university is particularly recognized for its College of Business and Economics, strong Education Department where many California teachers earn certification, and Music Department, including the California State University, East Bay Jazz Ensemble directed by Dave Eshelman (retired June 2007), which performs annually at Yoshi's in Oakland and tours Europe and South America. The Biotechnology Program has established CSUEB as a center for research and development in life sciences, bioinformatics, and related technologies in the Eastern San Francisco Bay Area. The university participates in the Internet2 project, a collaboration among over 200 U.S. universities, private industries, and governments to advance network technologies for research and higher education. It offers 48 undergraduate and 34 Master's degree programs, plus a teaching credential program, and a doctoral program in Educational Leadership (Ed.D.) in cooperation with the University of California, Berkeley, San Francisco State University, and San José State University. The most popular undergraduate majors among 2019 graduates include Business administration, Psychology, Health science, Kinesiology, Criminal justice, Biological sciences, Sociology, Computer science, Human development, and Fine art. The academic structure is organized into four colleges, including two Liberal Arts colleges and two vocational colleges. First-year students are placed in Freshman Learning Communities to support academic and social development. The university is ranked in the 2025–2026 USNWR Best Regional Colleges West Rankings and the 2024–2025 USNWR Graduate School Rankings. The Department of Communications publishes The Pioneer, a weekly student- and faculty-staffed newspaper named after the school's mascot, Pioneer Pete. CSUEB is diverse, with the largest enrollment percentage of Filipino Americans, the second largest of Pacific Islanders, African Americans, and non-residents in the Cal State system as of fall 2018. ASI, a student-run and student-owned organization, has a 15-member Board of Directors elected by students, which governs policy, oversees finances, and assists in planning campus programs and events. ASI has four departments: ASI Presents, ASI Business Office, Student Government, and the Early Childhood Education Center. In 2007 and 2008, the university administration denied ASI the right to hold student referendums on increasing fees for a recreation and wellness center and athletic scholarships for a move to Division II, instead allowing only 'alternative consultation'. The university's athletic teams are known as the Pioneers and compete in NCAA Division II, primarily in the California Collegiate Athletic Association (CCAA) since the 2009–10 academic year, with women's water polo competing in the Western Water Polo Association (WWPA). The Pioneers previously competed in the California Pacific Conference (Cal Pac) of the NAIA from 1998–99 to 2008–09. CSUEB competes in 15 varsity sports: men's sports include baseball, basketball, cross country, golf, soccer, and track & field (indoor and outdoor); women's sports include basketball, cross country, golf, soccer, softball, swimming, track & field (indoor and outdoor), volleyball, and water polo. The mascot was initially an astronaut in 1961, and the university has earned two NCAA Division II team championships, including a women's soccer championship in 1988. The NCAA Women's Water Polo Championship is open to all three NCAA divisions, with only East Bay and CSU Monterey Bay from the CCAA participating in the Western Water Polo Association.
